title: Percentage-Based DI
tagline: Year 2 — Tables where values are given as percentages of totals

introduction.overview: In a percentage-based DI set, the table gives totals and also percentages of those totals, for example the percentage of girls or the percentage who passed. To answer questions you must convert percentages into actual numbers by multiplying by the right total, and sometimes to convert back to a percentage of a different total. The key is to know which total each percentage refers to.
introduction.placementRelevance: Percentage-based DI sets are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, and they test accuracy with percentages more than speed of reading.
introduction.realWorldContext: Survey results, pass percentages and market shares are reported as percentages of different totals.

learningObjectives: Convert a percentage of a total into a number
Compute overall percentages from group data
Compare groups by numbers rather than by percentages
Compute ratios and differences from derived numbers

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Number = percentage ÷ 100 × total. The complement of x% is (100 − x)%. Overall percentage = total of parts ÷ total of wholes × 100.

coreDefinitions: Base (or total): the quantity that the percentage is a part of.
Derived column: a new column of numbers computed from percentages and totals.
Overall percentage: sum of parts ÷ sum of totals, not the average of percentages.
Percentage point difference: difference between two percentages.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A percentage is meaningless without its total. Once you convert every percentage to an actual number (a derived column), the rest of the problem is simple arithmetic on numbers. Averaging percentages directly gives wrong answers because the groups have different sizes.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Add derived columns to the table: girls, boys, passed. Do this once, then use the new columns to answer all questions.

mainNarrative: First, derive the numbers. College P has 1200 students of whom 40% are girls: 480 girls and 720 boys. 80% passed: 960 students. Do this for each college and write the numbers in new columns.

Compare using numbers, not percentages. College R has the highest pass percentage (90%) but only 800 students, so 720 passed. College S has only 60% pass rate but 2000 students, so 1200 passed, the most of any college.

For overall percentages, add the numbers: the total number of students is 6500 and the total number who passed is 960 + 1050 + 720 + 1200 + 750 = 4680, so the overall pass percentage is 4680 ÷ 6500 × 100 = 72%. The simple average of the five percentages would give 75%, which is wrong.
For ratios, use derived numbers: girls : boys in college T is 550 : 450 = 11 : 9.
Always check that the numbers are whole and sensible; a percentage of a total that gives a fraction of a person suggests a misread.

deepDiveAspects.title: Average of percentages is not overall
deepDiveAspects.content: Because groups differ in size, the overall percentage is a weighted average. Always go through the totals.

deepDiveAspects.title: Percentage points vs percent
deepDiveAspects.content: If the pass rate rises from 70% to 80%, it rises by 10 percentage points and by 14.3% in relative terms.

solvedExamples.title: Derived numbers
solvedExamples.question: How many girls are there in college P, and how many boys?

solvedExamples.title: Overall percentage
solvedExamples.question: What is the overall pass percentage of the five colleges together?

solvedExamples.title: Compare by number
solvedExamples.question: Which college had the highest number of students who passed?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A large college can lead even with a lower pass rate.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing R, which has the highest pass percentage.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Add columns for girls, boys and passed once. Use them for every later question.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Reject answers that treat a percentage as a number or vice versa.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Overall percentages are the usual trap.
